handbookNote: South Dakota Notary Public Law -- compiled from the official South Dakota Legislature source (sdlegislature.gov), retrieved directly (not AI-summarized) from SDCL Chapter 18-1 (Notaries Public), Chapter 18-4 (Acknowledgment and Proof of Instruments), Chapter 18-5 (Uniform Acknowledgment Law), and ARSD Chapter 5:04:03 (Secretary of State administrative rules); compiled source saved at temp/handbooks/sd/notary.txt. CLASSIFICATION: South Dakota is an application-only notary state for the standard commission -- there is no exam and no mandatory training/education course (confirmed both by the absence of any exam/course requirement anywhere in the fetched statute/rule text, and by the July 2025 SD Notary Public Handbook, NNA, and SOS materials; training is recommended, not required). This product is framed accordingly as a self-study/reference practice-question set grounded in real state notary law, not 'exam prep.' UNUSUAL FEATURES DOCUMENTED IN THIS TRACK: (1) A 2025 law (SL 2025, ch 90) removed South Dakota's surety-bond requirement for notaries entirely -- the current text of SDCL 18-1-2 and 18-1-3 requires only the statutory oath (SDCL 3-1-5) and an official seal filed with the secretary of state, with no bond language remaining (a very recent change, directly verifiable in the fetched current statute text). (2) South Dakota has TWO textually distinct remote-notarization methods, not one: (a) a 2019-era 'mail-based' video-witnessing method at SDCL 18-1-11.1 (enacted SL 2019, ch 100) for TANGIBLE documents, where the notary observes the signer via video communication technology using a personal-knowledge/familiarity identity standard, but must still affix signature to the original paper document (i.e., the document is physically mailed to the notary for wet-ink signature after the video session) -- certificate form at SDCL 18-4-29; and (b) full modern Remote Online Notarization (RON) at SDCL 18-1-11.2 through 18-1-11.8 (enacted 2024 via SL 2024, ch 71, i.e., 2024 SB 211), for ELECTRONIC records, requiring two-method identity proofing, a tamper-evident electronic notarization system (selected in advance and disclosed to the SOS per 18-1-11.4), and a 10-year audio-visual recording retention requirement (18-1-11.3) -- certificate form at SDCL 18-4-30. These two methods have materially different identity-verification standards and are frequently confused; this track tests the distinction directly. (3) Copy-certification is narrow, not general: the only copy-certification authority granted in the fetched chapters is the purpose-specific power to authenticate a PRINTED copy of an electronically-notarized RON record (SDCL 18-1-11.5, form at 18-1-11.6) -- South Dakota notaries do not have a general statutory power to certify true copies of arbitrary documents, unlike some other states' broader 'certified copy' notarial acts. (4) South Dakota notary name/home address is public record by statute -- this is general-background context from state open-records law (SDCL 1-27), not a provision located within chapters 18-1/18-4/18-5/ARSD 5:04:03, so it is documented here for institutional memory but was not converted into a graded MCQ (no specific citable section was fetched to ground a precise answer key). (5) No fee may ever be charged for notarizing a request for an absentee ballot (SDCL 18-1-9), while ordinary notarization fees are otherwise permissive, not mandatory. STATUTE COVERAGE: chapters are fragmented (not a unified RULONA chapter) but combined span roughly 71 operative sections after excluding repealed sections (23 in ch 18-1, 28 in ch 18-4, 18 in ch 18-5, 2 in ARSD 5:04:03) -- genuinely substantial once combined, consistent with the pre-build estimate of 40-55+ operative sections. CONTENT DEPTH: 126 grounded questions were generated across 8 topic buckets (commission/application/seal; definitions; notarial duties/fees/misdemeanors; video communication notarization; remote online notarization; acknowledgment and proof of instruments; certificate forms; Uniform Acknowledgment Law) -- within the 120-160 target range, each question citing a specific SDCL/ARSD section and grounded in verbatim fetched statute text; no padding or invented facts were used to hit a target ('better nothing than nonsense' per site owner directive). PRICING: $0.75 (75 cents) -- the low end of this project's pricing scale, reflecting a genuinely thin single-purpose application-only state track (no exam, no course) rather than a full licensing-exam prep product.
